content: Superatoms are clusters of atoms that exhibit properties similar to those of individual elemental atoms. When sodium atoms are cooled from a vapor state, they naturally condense into clusters containing specific numbers of atoms, such as 2, 8, 20, 40, 58, or 92. These specific numbers are referred to as magic numbers. The first two of these numbers correspond to the number of electrons required to fill the s and p orbitals, respectively. In these clusters, the electrons behave as if they belong to the entire cluster rather than to individual atoms. However, deviations can occur in non-spherical or doped clusters, as the potential is influenced by the shape of the positive nuclei. Superatoms tend to exhibit chemical behavior that allows them to achieve a closed shell of electrons under this new counting scheme. For instance, a superatom with one extra electron beyond a full shell will easily lose that electron, behaving similarly to an alkali metal. Conversely, a cluster with one electron short of a full shell will have a high electron affinity, resembling the behavior of halogens. Certain aluminum clusters also display superatomic properties. For example, when clusters of 13 aluminum atoms (Al₁₃) are reacted with iodine gas in a helium environment, the primary reaction product is Al₁₃I⁻. This cluster, with an additional electron, does not react with oxygen when introduced into the same gas stream. Assuming each aluminum atom contributes its three valence electrons, the cluster contains 40 electrons, which is one of the magic numbers observed in sodium clusters. This suggests that these magic numbers reflect the stability associated with noble gas configurations. Computational studies indicate that the additional electron in the Al₁₃I⁻ cluster is located opposite the iodine atom, implying that the aluminum cluster has a higher electron affinity than iodine. As a result, the aluminum cluster is referred to as a superhalogen. The Al₁₃ component in the Al₁₃I⁻ ion behaves chemically like an iodine ion or, more accurately, a bromine atom. Similarly, the Al₁₃I₂⁻ cluster is expected to exhibit chemical behavior akin to the triiodide ion. Clusters of 14 aluminum atoms (Al₁₄) with 42 electrons (two more than a magic number) exhibit properties similar to alkaline earth metals, which typically adopt a +2 valence state. This behavior is observed only when at least three iodine atoms are attached to the Al₁₄ cluster, forming Al₁₄I₃⁻. The anionic cluster has a total of 43 itinerant electrons, but the three iodine atoms each remove one electron, leaving 40 electrons in the jellium shell. Atomic clusters of inert gas atoms are particularly easy and reliable to study using computer simulations. The interaction between two atoms can be well-approximated using the Lennard-Jones potential. Other computational methods are also available, and it has been established that the magic numbers for inert gas clusters include 13, 19, 23, 26, 29, 32, 34, 43, 46, 49, 55, and so on. As more superatoms are discovered that mimic the properties of specific atoms, a new branch of study is emerging, potentially leading to the development of a three-dimensional periodic table.
